name: Design a Service Mesh
intent: Give hundreds of microservices secure, observable and resilient calls to each other by moving that work out of the application code and into proxies that a control plane configures.
codeTitle: a client-side proxy with least-request balancing, ejection and a retry budget
finalIntro: One call from service A to service B through the mesh.
prompt: Design a service mesh for a company with 400 microservices, written in four languages and running on Kubernetes. Every call between services should be encrypted and authenticated, balanced across healthy pods, retried safely, limited, measured and traceable, and the platform team should be able to change the rules without asking 400 teams to redeploy.
functional: Encrypt every service-to-service call and prove which service is calling
Allow or deny calls by policy, for example only the checkout service may call payments
Balance calls across the pods of the target service, and stop sending to bad pods
Apply timeouts, retries and circuit breaking to calls, without changing application code
Shift a share of the traffic to a new version of a service for a canary release
Limit the request rate to a service, per caller if needed
Record metrics, access logs and trace headers for every call
nonFunctional: Add no more than about 1 to 2 ms of median latency per hop, and a small share of CPU and memory per pod
A configuration change reaches every affected proxy within seconds
The mesh must never be a single point of failure: if the control plane is down, calls keep working with the last configuration
Certificates are short-lived (hours), rotate by themselves and never need an engineer
Work for any language and for services that nobody wants to touch
A mistake in a mesh-wide setting must not be able to take every service down at once

firstAttempt.text: Each team uses a client library in its own language for calls to other services. The library handles timeouts and retries with its own defaults, TLS is optional and set up by hand with certificates that last a year, load balancing is a DNS name behind a cluster IP, and each team writes its own metrics and logs.
limits: Four languages mean four implementations of retries, timeouts and balancing, each with different bugs and defaults
Changing a rule, such as a timeout, needs a code change and a deploy of every service that makes the call
Year-long certificates are copied around by hand, and an expired one takes a service down in the middle of the night
Retries at every layer multiply, since no one sees the whole chain, and one slow service can start a retry storm
A cluster IP balances connections, not requests, so one long-lived connection sends all its traffic to one pod
Metrics and traces are missing wherever a team forgot, so an incident has gaps in exactly the wrong place

steps.title: Put a proxy next to every service and send all traffic through it
steps.problem: Retries, timeouts, encryption and balancing are re-implemented in every language and every team, and cannot be changed without redeploying the application.
steps.fix: Run a small L7 proxy, such as Envoy, in every pod as a sidecar container. Rules in the pod's network namespace redirect all traffic in and out of the application through it, so the application still calls http://payments and does not know the proxy exists. The proxy of the caller picks the target and applies the policies, and the proxy of the callee receives the call and applies its own. The mesh features are now the same for every language, and they are changed by changing proxy configuration, not application code.
steps.tradeoff: One implementation serves every service, and it can be updated without touching the applications. Each call now crosses two extra processes, which costs about 0.5 ms each at the median and some memory and CPU in every pod, and the proxy has to start before the application and be upgraded with it.

steps.title: Let a control plane push the configuration to every proxy
steps.problem: Hundreds of proxies need to know where every service's pods are right now, and the rules for each, and nobody can edit them by hand.
steps.fix: A control plane, such as Istiod, watches the Kubernetes API and the mesh rules that the platform team writes as declarative objects. It turns them into proxy configuration (routes, clusters, endpoints, listeners) and streams it to each proxy over xDS, a gRPC protocol where the proxy subscribes and the server sends only what changed. A new pod is in every interested proxy's list within seconds. The proxies keep running with their last configuration if the control plane disappears.
steps.tradeoff: One place to describe the rules for the whole fleet, with fast and incremental updates. The control plane is now a powerful component: a bad rule goes everywhere, and its memory and CPU grow with the number of proxies and endpoints, so each proxy should be told only about the services it really calls.

steps.title: Give every workload an identity and encrypt all calls with short-lived certificates
steps.problem: Without identity, any pod in the network can call any service, and anyone who can read the network can read the traffic.
steps.fix: Each pod's proxy proves who it is to the control plane with the pod's Kubernetes service account token, and the mesh certificate authority signs a short-lived X.509 certificate that names the workload, for example spiffe://shop/ns/payments/sa/payments. The proxies use these certificates to set up mutual TLS: both sides prove who they are and the traffic is encrypted. Certificates last hours and are renewed halfway through, by the proxy, without a restart. Because the callee's proxy now knows who is calling, an authorization policy can say that only the checkout identity may POST to /charge on payments, and everything else is denied.
steps.tradeoff: Encryption and authentication come for free for every service, and a stolen certificate is useless within hours. The certificate authority and its root key become critical secrets, handshakes add CPU and a little latency (kept low by reusing connections), and every pod needs a valid certificate to take part in the mesh.

steps.title: Make calls resilient: balance, time out, retry within a budget, eject bad pods, limit the rate
steps.problem: Calls fail and slow down all the time, and the naive reaction, retrying everywhere, turns a small problem into an outage.
steps.fix: The caller's proxy balances every request, not every connection, usually with least-request (or power of two choices) and a preference for pods in the same zone. Each route has a timeout and a retry policy: retry only safe failures, with a short backoff, and only while retries are below a budget such as 20% of the live requests, so that a failing service gets at most a little extra load. Outlier detection ejects a pod after a few consecutive errors for a while, and connection and request limits act as a circuit breaker. A rate limit service holds the counters for global limits, for example per caller.
steps.tradeoff: Failures are hidden and contained in a uniform way, and the budget bounds the amplification. Retries still need idempotent operations, a timeout and retry policy per route has to be chosen with care, and a limit that is too tight rejects good traffic. Without a budget and a sensible timeout at each layer a mesh makes a retry storm worse, not better.

steps.title: Shift traffic by weight for canary releases
steps.problem: A new version of a service should see real traffic gradually, and be rolled back in seconds if it is wrong, without a deploy.
steps.fix: The new version runs as separate pods with a version label. A route rule sends a weight of the traffic to each version, for example 95/5 and then 80/20 and 50/50, and it can also match on a header so that testers always reach the new one. Because the rule is part of the configuration that the control plane pushes, a change takes effect in seconds in every caller's proxy, and the metrics of the mesh show the error rate and latency of each version side by side. An automatic controller can promote the canary, or roll it back if its error rate is worse.
steps.tradeoff: Releases become gradual, measurable and reversible, independently of deploying the code. The percentages are per caller proxy and per request, so a user may see both versions, and the old and new version must be compatible with each other and with the same database.

steps.title: Record metrics, logs and trace headers for every call
steps.problem: Finding why a request was slow or failed in a chain of 12 services needs the same data from every service, which hand-written instrumentation never provides.
steps.fix: Every proxy sees every request and response, so it emits the golden signals itself: request count, error rate and a latency histogram, labelled with the source and destination service and the response code. It writes an access log line with the identities, the route, the status, the time spent and the number of retries, and it starts or continues a trace by creating spans and forwarding the trace headers (W3C traceparent or B3). The application only has to copy the incoming trace headers onto its outgoing calls. A collector aggregates the data, with sampling for logs and traces and full counts for metrics.
steps.tradeoff: Uniform data for the whole fleet from day one, with a service graph for free, and no gaps where a team forgot. The volume is large at 100% (metrics have many label combinations and logs are huge), traces are broken wherever an application drops the headers, and the proxies spend CPU on it.

failures.impact: No new endpoints, routes or certificates can be pushed, so changes stop, but if the proxies stopped working too, every call in the company would stop.
failures.answer: The proxies are the data plane and keep running with the last configuration they received, including the endpoint lists and the certificates they hold, so existing calls continue. Pods that are replaced during the outage are not seen until it is back, and certificates that expire during it would break, which is why they live for hours and are renewed at half their life, and why the control plane runs several replicas across zones with alerts on its health.

failures.scenario: A bad configuration is pushed to every proxy
failures.impact: A wrong route, a timeout of 1 ms or a policy that denies everything is applied to the whole fleet in seconds, which is the same speed that makes the mesh useful.
failures.answer: The control plane validates the rule before it is pushed, and the proxy rejects configuration it cannot load and keeps the previous one. Mesh-wide changes are rolled out like code: reviewed in version control, applied first to a test namespace, then a few services, then the rest, with the error rate watched and a one-step rollback. The most dangerous defaults, such as retries and timeouts, are set per route with limits, not as one global value.

failures.scenario: A slow service starts a retry storm
failures.impact: In a chain of 4 services each of the 3 hops makes up to 4 tries (3 retries), so 1 user request can become 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 requests to the service at the bottom, which is already struggling and now gets far more load than before.
failures.answer: Retries are limited by a budget (a share of the live traffic) and use backoff with jitter, circuit breaking and outlier ejection stop sending to a failing service, and the timeouts get smaller, not larger, deeper in the chain. Retrying is done at one layer where possible, and only for idempotent requests. Load is shed with a clear error that is not retried instead of queueing without limit.

failures.scenario: Certificates expire or the certificate authority is unavailable
failures.impact: Proxies reject each other's handshakes, so calls fail with TLS errors across many services at the same time.
failures.answer: Certificates are renewed when half their life is over, so a failure of the authority has hours to be fixed before anything expires, and renewal is retried with backoff and alerts. The root key is kept offline or in a hardware module, with an intermediate that is rotated. Clocks are synchronised, a metric of the time left on certificates is alerted on, and the authority runs redundantly.

failures.scenario: The application starts before its sidecar is ready, or the sidecar dies
failures.impact: The first calls from a new pod fail because outbound traffic is redirected to a proxy that is not listening, and a pod that is shutting down loses its last calls.
failures.answer: The pod is not started until the proxy is ready: the proxy container is started first and the application waits for its readiness check. On shutdown the application drains first and the proxy exits last. Resource requests and limits are set for the proxy, and health checks restart it if it hangs.

alternatives.title: Where the proxy runs

options.name: A sidecar in every pod
options.pro: Strong isolation per workload, full L7 features and the most mature model
options.con: Memory and CPU in every pod, an extra process to start and upgrade, and about 1 ms per hop

options.name: One proxy per node (ambient mesh)
options.pro: Much less memory and no restart of the application to join or upgrade, with L4 mTLS from a shared node proxy and L7 features only where a waypoint is deployed
options.con: A shared proxy is a bigger blast radius per node, and L7 policy needs an extra hop through a waypoint

options.name: A library in the application (Finagle, gRPC)
options.pro: No extra hop at all, and the lowest latency
options.con: One implementation per language, upgrades need a redeploy of every service, and services nobody can change are left out

alternatives.pick: Sidecars for fine-grained L7 control and the most proven path; ambient to cut cost where mostly mTLS and simple routing are needed; a library only for a few languages and a team that owns every service.

alternatives.title: How the traffic is balanced

options.name: Round robin
options.pro: Simple and fair when requests cost the same
options.con: Ignores slow pods, so a slow pod keeps getting its full share

options.name: Least request (or power of two choices)
options.pro: Sends less to busy pods, which adapts to slowness with no extra signals
options.con: Needs a per-proxy count of requests in flight, which each proxy sees only for its own traffic

options.name: Consistent hash on a header
options.pro: The same key always reaches the same pod, which helps caches
options.con: Uneven load when a key is hot

alternatives.pick: Least request with zone preference as the default, and hashing only for services that cache by key.

alternatives.title: How to identify a caller

options.name: mTLS with workload certificates (SPIFFE)
options.pro: The identity is proved by the connection itself and the application never handles credentials
options.con: Needs a certificate authority and rotation, and identity is of the workload, not of the end user

options.name: Signed tokens (JWT) in a header
options.pro: Can carry the end user and claims, and passes through proxies and queues
options.con: The application or proxy must validate and refresh them, and a stolen token works anywhere until it expires

options.name: Network rules by IP address
options.con: Pod addresses change constantly and an address is not an identity

alternatives.pick: mTLS for service identity, and JWT on top for the end user.

alternatives.title: Whether to adopt a mesh at all

options.name: A full mesh
options.pro: Uniform security, resilience and telemetry for hundreds of services in many languages
options.con: A large system to run, to learn and to debug, with a cost per pod

options.name: An API gateway and shared libraries
options.pro: Much simpler, and enough for a few dozen services in one or two languages
options.con: Only the edge is covered, and each service still has to do the rest

options.name: Only mTLS and policy at the node or network level
options.pro: Gets the security benefits with little overhead
options.con: No per-request retries, routing or L7 metrics

alternatives.pick: A mesh from about 50 to 100 services, or earlier when the rules must be uniform across languages; before that, a gateway and one good library.

roles.label: Application services
roles.description: The microservices that make and receive the calls, and know nothing about the mesh.

roles.label: Proxies
roles.description: The sidecar proxies and the rate limit service on the path of every call.

roles.label: Telemetry
roles.description: The collector that receives metrics, logs and spans from every proxy.

roles.label: Control plane
roles.description: Computes the configuration and pushes it to the proxies over xDS.

roles.label: Registry, certificates and stores
roles.description: The service registry, the certificate authority and the metrics and trace store.

quiz.question: A company with 400 services in four languages needs to lower the default timeout on calls to the payments service within minutes, without asking each team to redeploy. Which approach achieves it?
options: Release a new version of the shared client library in each of the four languages and ask teams to upgrade
Store the timeout in a config map that each service reads at start-up and roll the value out gradually
Run a sidecar proxy in every pod and have a control plane push the new route timeout to all proxies over xDS in seconds
Set the timeout on the Kubernetes cluster IP service of payments so kube-proxy enforces it for callers
quiz.explanation: Sidecars make timeouts and retries proxy configuration, so changes reach every caller in seconds without touching application code. Library or config-map changes need redeploys or restarts and four implementations. A cluster IP balances connections, not requests, and does not enforce per-request timeouts.

quiz.question: In a chain of three services, each hop makes up to 3 tries (2 retries) before giving up, and the bottom service is slow. How many requests can one user request cause at the bottom, and what limits the damage best?
options: Up to 9, and raising each hop's timeout so that fewer tries are needed is enough to keep the extra load in check
Up to 27, and a retry budget of about 20 percent of live traffic with backoff, retrying at one layer, caps it
Up to 27, and adding a fixed 200 ms delay between retries spreads the load enough to protect the bottom service
Up to 6, since each hop adds only two retries
quiz.explanation: Tries multiply across hops: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. A retry budget bounds the extra load whatever the depth. A fixed delay only spaces out the same 27 requests, and adding the tries instead of multiplying them is the usual miscount.

quiz.question: A platform engineer pushes a mesh-wide route with a 1 ms timeout. Within seconds, errors appear across hundreds of services. The team wants to keep changing rules in seconds. What is the best change to the process?
options: Validate rules first, roll out in stages with error rates watched and a one-step rollback, and set risky values per route
Delay every change by an hour in the control plane, so there is always time to notice a mistake before it spreads across the whole fleet
Require sign-off from the owners of all 400 services before any mesh-wide rule is pushed
Run two control planes and push each change through both, comparing outputs before proxies apply it
quiz.explanation: Treating mesh config like code, with validation, staged rollout, metrics and rollback, keeps the speed and limits the blast radius. A fixed delay removes the speed benefit and does not stop a bad rule. Sign-off from 400 teams defeats the purpose, and two control planes fed the same rule would both push the same mistake.
